To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the light particles emitted from Ar+Ni reactions at 95A  MeV have the following properties: 1) The light particle emission is prompt, i.e., the light particles are emitted during the collision and not from the evaporation of excited nuclear residues; 2) The light particles are emitted from the projectile, the target and the intermediate mass fragments; 3) The light particle multiplicity is correlated with the mass and the charge of the projectile-like and target-like fragments; and

the properties of light particles (pions, protons, and neutrons) emitted in Ar+Ni collisions at 95A meV are consistent with a picture of a very hot, dense fireball, which is formed at a very early stage of the reaction.

the emission of particles from the projectile-like and target-like nuclei is not correlated, that the evaporation of light particles from the projectile is not correlated with the emission of the same particles from the target nucleus, and that the emission of light particles from both the projectile and the target nuclei is not correlated with that from the projectile-like or target-like nuclei.

the production and properties of light charged particles in collisions of 95A Me V 40Ar with a thick Ni target.
the properties of light particles (protons, neutrons and deuterons) emitted in the reaction of Ar+Ni at an incident energy of 95A Mev, as a function of the impact parameter.
the study of the production of light particles (LP) in the Ar+Ni reaction at 95A  MeV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the light particle properties of 95A Me V Ar + Ni collisions are consistent with a two-component picture, in which the light particles emitted from the projectile-like fragment are emitted in a prompt manner and are characterized by the emission of a large fraction of neutrons and protons, while those emitted from the target-like fragment are emitted from a hot and equilibrated source, characterized by a high neutron/proton ratio and a low kinetic energy.
the emission of the light charged particles is a complex phenomenon that is not fully understood.

it has been possible to identify, in the light particle emission, the prompt component of the evaporation residue and to separate the evaporation residue from the light particles produced in the primary interaction.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the light particles produced in Ar + Ni collisions at 95A meV are not emitted from a single source, but are emitted from two different sources.

the emission of light particles (protons, neutrons and pions) in heavy-ion collisions is not only a consequence of the decay of the primary fragments but is also a direct consequence of the nuclear reaction.
